KEY MESSAGE 1...
A slow moving cold front finally gets a kick and moves through our 
area north to south this afternoon showers and a few storms. Some 
storms could get a bit on the stronger side, but the primary 
limiting factor to that will be a displaced instability axis 
from the highest shear. The belt of strongest mid-level flow, 
and thus deep layer shear, will be in the northern half of our 
area. The best opportunity for heating and better instability 
will be in the southern half of our area in the thinner cloud 
cover out ahead of the front. REFS joint probability for >500 
J/kg of SBCAPE and >30 knots of shear to capture the best 
overlap of parameters has shifted a bit farther northwest in 
several iterations of runs with around 60- 90% from eastern OH, 
through far southwestern PA, and into northern WV. A handful of 
recent HRRR and RRFS MPAS runs favor a slightly slower moving 
front and thus storms firing a bit farther north, which is 
falling more in line with the REFS shift, so this could be a 
trend to note through the day today. So, this will be the area 
to watch for storms to get more feisty and bring a low-end 
damaging wind threat coincident with SPC's Marginal Risk. Hail 
seems less likely with thinner CAPE profiles within the hail 
growth zone and a too shallow equilibrium level capping updrafts
before they can maximize on hail growth. With lacking low level
lapse rates progged by the latest RAP, we'd likely need to see 
the deep layer shear organize and congeal the storms into 
clusters to capitalize on the wind threat. Can't entirely rule 
out some flash flood concern which would be a bit more 
concerning if storms do fire farther north and impact 
southwestern Pennsylvania where two rounds of storms already 
went through earlier in the morning and preconditioned the 
ground, but that's still favored in southern OH and northern WV.

KEY MESSAGE 2...
The most impactful system arrives on Friday ushering in strong wind 
gusts, well below normal temperatures, and showers. While some 
uncertainty remains among ensembles primarily owing to timing and, 
to a lesser extent, depth of the mid-level trough, confidence in all 
three impacts remains high. Deep surface low pressure will pull a 
cold front through the area on Friday with a tight pressure 
gradient, 10+ dam 500 mb height falls in 12 hours, and strong low-
level cold advection.

For the wind threat, the combination of the tight gradient and 
mixing into a 40-45 knot low level jet should result in widespread 
gusts of 35-45 mph. They'll be stronger across our higher elevation 
remains up to ~60%. The already low probability of Advisory criteria 
in the lowlands has decreased a bit to only around 20-40%, so while 
still not likely, not entirely out of the question either. Eastern 
Tucker County runs an elevated probability for High Wind Warning 
criteria gusts >58 mph also up to ~60%. Wind headlines for the 
ridges will likely come into consideration within the next 24-36 
hours.

Strong cold advection in post-frontal northwest flow will bottom out 
ensemble mean 850 mb temperatures to around -2 to -4C. An 
unseasonably cold air mass will settle in for the first half of
the weekend providing the potential for two nights of frost and
freeze. Friday night, it looks like a freeze or bust as wind 
will remain elevated in the post-frontal regime. So, while 
probabilities for <36F lows are high, especially outside of 
urban areas, not too concerned about widespread frost. Probs for
<32F (and an unconditional freeze) sneak up to 40-50% along and
north of I-80, so that'll be the area to worry about on Friday 
night. Saturday daytime highs will feel more like those of mid 
to late November only warming to near 50 degrees with 40s in the
elevation. The gradient will relax some Sunday night allowing 
wind to slacken and skies will clear. This should point toward 
Saturday night being the coldest areawide, and possibly the 
first shot for the Pittsburgh climate site to dip to 32F or 
lower since May 2nd. With better radiational cooling conditions 
amid a dry, cold airmass, the dew point could essentially be the
floor for lows, and this suggests widespread low to mid 30s and
upper 20s. A widespread frost is likely. Probability for a 
freeze ranges from 40-80% in eastern OH, northern WV, and 
western PA, with the highest values away from urban areas and in
the higher elevation. Expect that we'll be looking at some 
combination of frost/freeze headlines on top of wind headlines 
as well.

Two rounds of precip are possible both along the front itself and 
then in the wrap around cold advection across the lakes on Saturday. 
Strong flow amid the dynamic system could drive some "power showers" 
accompanying FROPA on Friday bringing enhanced gusts with them 
provided they're able to get tall enough to tap into the 40-50 knots
